title: Acquisition Topics Cyber Test and Evaluation for Supply Chain Risk Management 11.9.21

cues.text: >> I'd like to welcome everybody to today's DAU event.
We have the Cyber Testing Evaluation for Supply Chain Risk Management.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
We also have Miss Elly Millar as our host.
The agenda for today.
Microphones will be muted.
The session is being recorded.
It will be posted to dau.edu/dau-webcast which is at the bottom.
We are taking questions today.
Please submit your questions via the chat.
We will respond verbally to your questions so -- towards the end of the event.
There is a survey at the end.
We will post the survey link in the chat.
Takes a couple minutes to fill out.
We would appreciate it.
If you're here for CLPs, the session does qualify for up
to 1.5 CLPs with supervisor approval.
It is not automatic.
You will need to apply for it.
There is a link at the end of the survey that you can copy and paste
to get your CLP certificate and to present to your supervisor for approval.
Now I'm going to turn it over to Miss Elly Millar.
>> Welcome everybody to today's webcast: Cyber Testing Evaluation
for Supply Chain Risk Management.
My name as Emmett has introduced is Elly Millar, and I'm your host for today's event.
Before I introduce you to our guest speaker, I'm going to take a few minutes to introduce you
to the DAU Cybersecurity Enterprise Team and capabilities.
Cybersecurity Enterprise Team is federated across US
in about eight different fiscal locations attached to one of these four regions
that you see, which enables us to support all of our customers virtually or in person.
In addition to providing cybersecurity courses and workshops,
we assist organizations solve cyber challenges through consulting, embed or through short-
and long-term mission assistance.
Our faculty members have real world, private-sector, and you'd experience backed
by industry certifications and continuing education to deliver cybersecurity education
and consulting in the many different areas such as Cloud Security, Cybersecurity,
Maturity Model Certification, Cyber Test and Evaluation,
Cyber Resiliency Engineering to highlight a few.
You can find our course offerings and register
on DAU's cornerstone on demand website dau.csod.com.
Some of these courses are part of our credentials.
There are currently two credentials online: Program Protection and Cybersecurity
for Program Managers credentials.
And we're in the process of developing Cyber Resiliency Introduction
and Practitioner Credentials.
We also offer various workshop as listed here on the left side.
If you are defense industry or partners, you may be interested
in the Cybersecurity Maturity Model certification and DFARS training,
which is offered in many different formats on a regular basis.
Cyber training range is a unique workshop we offer here at DAU.
It's 90% hands on where you get to use open-source tools such as Kali Linux
and Metasploit to hack business systems, as well as a weapons system all in virtual environment.
We currently offer it twice a month virtually.
It's intended for a broader audience to gain a better understanding
of how cyber adversaries think so we can do better defense.
Absolutely no experience necessary.
We also conduct cyber tabletop workshops.
Cyber tabletop is one of the mission-based cyber risk assessments
which is directed by DOD 5009.89.
If you didn't know already, DOD cyber tabletop guide version two came out in September
of this year, and we have updated the workshop to reflect the changes.
In this workshop, you'll gain foundational knowledge on cyber tabletop methodology as well
as attack surface characterizations through discussions and exercises.
And taking this workshop is the first step in getting certified as a CTT facilitator,
and it's offered once a month virtually.
You can register for both cyber training range and cyber tabletop workshop again
on DAU's Cornerstone on demand website.
Lastly, we're currently working with NAVAIR to build the Advanced Cyber Training Range.
What you see in the picture are fiscal benches in our mid-Atlantic campus.
There are from left to right automotive bench, avionics bench, and navigation bench
where you'll have the opportunity to test and hack
into these systems using non-traditional protocols such as CAN [phonetic]
and 1553 bus [phonetic] in person, so please stay tuned
for our advanced cyber training range workshop.
If you have any questions regarding any of our offerings or collaboration opportunities,
please email us at cybersecurity@dau.edu and also check
out DAU Cybersecurity Community of Practice.
Today's presentation regarding Cyber Testing Evaluation
for Supply Chain Risk Management is a very important topic.
It was reported that supply chain attacks rose by 42% in the fourth quarter of 2021
in US impacting up to 7 million people and the problem is global.
The European Union cybersecurity agency who is the body responsible
for European level coordinated actions on cybersecurity and emerging technologies
like artificial intelligence and 5G conducted a study
on 24 supply chain attacks from January 2020 to July 2021.
They found that supply chain attacks are getting more sophisticated
and more advanced persistent threat actors are conducting the attacks,
making traditional cybersecurity measures insufficient to defend
against supply chain cyber threats.
So, what does this mean for DOD warfighting capabilities?
Miss Sarah Standard joins us today to present cyber testing evaluation strategies
and activities to address cyber threats to supply chain of DOD weapons systems.
Miss Standard is a retired Navy captain.
Her carrier includes instructing calculus and cybersecurity at Naval Academy,
as well as teaching cyber warfare at NAVAIR.
In 2016, she transitioned to serve as the Cybersecurity
and Interoperability Technical Director.
And now she's the Director for Developmental Test Evaluation and Assessments in the office
of Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering.
What I would add to that is that there isn't a cybersecurity effort, especially at the USD
and joint level that doesn't have her fingerprints on it.
She's either championing it or advocating for it,
which goes to show you her great passion for DOD and cybersecurity.
So, without further ado, Sarah, over to you.
>> Wow, what a great introduction.
I am not the Director for Developmental Test Evaluation Assessments.
I do work for him, though.
So, I appreciate that.
Okay, so welcome everybody.
And thank you for making the time today to come.
And thanks to DAU for the opportunity to present.
Can I get a confirmation that you can see my slides?
>>Yes, Sarah.
>> Awesome.
Okay. So, with that introduction, I guess I don't have anything else to say on this slide.
But I'm really happy to be here and look forward to your questions.
So, bottom line up front, I would like to present some draft guidance that is designed
to help perform cyber test and evaluation that focuses on preventing, identifying, mitigating
and deterring cyberspace threats to the supply chain.
So, these are cyber supply chain focus types of threats that we're focused on.
My focus obviously, is on DOD acquisition programs, and in particular weapons systems,
and on the DOD cyber test and evaluation processes, which include hardware,
firmware and software insurance, which, of course,
are integral to reducing risk in cyber supply chain.
While I will focus on the motivation behind this guidance and the approach itself.
I'm on slide three now.
So, supply -- the unique attributes of the supply chain, which I would like to discuss
as our motivation for this guidance, very complex, complicated attack surfaces.
When you look at your end product, your system and its attack surface, it's a very --
well, it's pretty much not as infinite,
or seemingly as infinite as the supply chain itself.
So, we'll take a look at that a little bit more.
Understanding, as Elly mentioned, you know, this global nature of supply chain risk,
and we're all in a supply chain crisis right now, of course in our country is.
So, global web of interconnected suppliers, manufacturers,
all the way down to those mom-and-pop shops that everyone likes to talk
about the mom-and-pop store fronts.
You know, the transportation, the infrastructure, all of these have massive,
unknown and undiscovered dependencies for DOD weapons systems and DOD systems in general.
It's a very dynamic supply chain.
It's very dynamic, always changing.
And it's very hard to perform that identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover,
the cybersecurity framework that NIST has published, against the supply chain.
Timing is unbounded, and we are being targeted by advanced threats.
I'm going on to Slide four.
So, on the right-hand side, this depiction is called a wheel of access.
And the Air Force first developed a wheel of access and we have modified it and expanded it
to add the critical infrastructure component, and add developmental
and test environments, processes, and tools.
So, this is also generalized so that any system can be considered in this wheel have access.
And when you take a look at this wheel of access and you think about the supply chain,
every single element, every single component, every single little spot on this data,
whether it be data, whether it be a system, piece of hardware, firmware, it --
they all have their own supply chains.
And that makes it overwhelmingly exponential in trying to understand where that risk could be.
So, this -- the hardware, the firmware, the software components can all be modified,
and we have to try to get our hands on this.
And we propose that cyber test evaluation can help.
Understanding that the development and test environments, processes, and tools are not part
of the program managers, like tested evaluation master plan won't be documenting
that necessarily, but you need a strategy to understand what those environments,
those processes, and tools might introduce in terms of risk through the supply chain.
On slide five.
I'm going to break down now into each of those areas -- those attributes, so very dynamic.
So, supply chain is constantly evolving.
There are market forces on suppliers,
they change their designs, they change what they're doing.
They aren't bounded to make it the same way for DOD every time, right?
They have profit and loss drivers.
They have mergers and acquisitions.
All the time, things are constantly changing.
And that the business relationships they have, who they're trusting, all those,
again, are continuously changing.
And disruptions to the supply chain cause the dynamic aspect
of the supply chain to evolve as well.
You've got ransomware, we saw the Columbia Pipeline and how that disrupt the gas supplies
on the East Coast, everybody panicking going out and buying, you know,
tons of gas, so they wouldn't have no gas.
And then we're seeing this -- all those ships that sitting out on the coast of California
with because we don't have enough drivers to handle the influx.
Those aren't even supplied cyber supply chain problems, right?
Well, this, the Columbia Pipeline was but what's going on on the east
on the West Coast is not the same as what can happen in cyberspace.
So, those disruptions in cyberspace are a big, you know, big concern and they're growing.
Ransomware is predicted to grow even greater in 2022.
War, natural disasters like the pandemic are in, they all can cause disruptions and the --
even the mergers and acquisitions can change -- can disrupt your supply chain.
Those trust relationships, who that particular company trusts, that changes.
The ownership changes.
The investors change.
Who's writing the code changes.
The technology itself and the digital ecosystem, whether they're using --
when they move to the commercial cloud and how well they're securing that environment.
We hear a lot of times in the open-source news about you know, commercial cloud configurations
by the you know, whoever is using that commercial cloud,
causing an exposure and a data breach.
And then, yeah, so the workforce.
The foreign coders.
How do we know we have foreign coders that we don't want writing code on our system?
Moving on to slide six.
So, it's very difficult to detect supply chain attacks.
And they're -- they can be much more sophisticated.
.They can happen from any point in the design to development to production.
And they may or may not show up at the time of testing.
They may be set to actively evade detection, lying dormant without any observable behavior
until a trigger that the adversary themselves has pre-planned and pre-programmed is activated.
And they can happen in any part of the system.
So, we tend to focus a lot on our critical parts.
But even our non-critical parts can facilitate a compromise
to the critical functionality of the system.
And anytime we do software updates, we don't always know could there be you know,
this is a perfect example of SolarWinds.
Right? How do you know that your software is not compromised?
And the challenge is that these threats are not something the intelligence community can have
knowledge of in advance.
They can happen, you know, one day there's no threat.
The very next day, now you have a breach.
So, this complex interaction between these components in our systems, the hardware,
the software and the firmware, that supply chain complexity is manifested in that complexity
of how these things work together as well.
Moving on to slide seven.
So anytime, anyplace, is when we can have a supply chain compromise to be --
unless we've really understood where the risks might come from.
So, supply chain compromises may show up at any point in your acquisition lifecycle
and through daily updates, as we talked about before and this notion of trust,
we talked about -- I mentioned earlier as well,
any supplier at any tier can be targeted by an advanced threat actor.
And it's a matter of that advanced threat actor understanding who is involved
in our supply chain, sometimes perhaps better than us.
So, they can have an ongoing presence on that lower tier supplier
that we don't have visibility into.
They can have a dormant implant there that won't be triggered in test.
And they can also be attacking other lower tier trusted suppliers
that aren't even in our supply chain of interest.
So, when we look at this term, trusted supplier and we think about how we're inheriting trust
or forwarding that trust up our supply chain, it's a tough thing to get your head around.
Because the adversaries in cyberspace, exploit trust.
That's exactly the thing they go after.
So, the more we trust, the more challenges we have.
So, current, you know, trend toward zero trust.
Will that help?
We certainly hope so.
But there is no silver bullet in this case.
The DOD does have efforts around building and maintaining trust within the supply chain.
The CIO is working that and so there is there are efforts,
but we're we still have a ways to go.
Moving on to slide eight.
So, there are tools that we know of that can help mitigate supply chain risk.
The first tool is having visibility into your supply chain.
There are automated tools that can support that threat characterization
and the supply chain illumination and automated capability
to continually illuminate your supply chain, which is critical if you want to be able
to understand the supply chain's attack surface.
So, attack surface characterization is another tool that you need in your toolbox
for mitigating supply chain risk.
You use -- informed by obviously, Criticality Analysis, an important aspect
of understanding your attack -- the attack surface of the supply chain,
but also mission based cyber risk assessments which you heard Elly mention at the beginning.
The cyber tabletop being one example.
Usually, every cyber tabletop will include supply chain analysis and attacks
through the supply chain proposed during those events.
So, in terms of contract requirements, that is another tool
to hold our contractors accountable.
DOD needs to do that.
We need to hold our contractors accountable.
Having a slowdown requirement of the clauses that we include.
So, there are many DFARS and FAR clauses that are either in the works or in place
that can help with holding the contractor accountable with respect to supply chain risk.
And I encourage programs to use those.
The challenge is that those contract requirements don't include cyber tests
and evaluation.
So, that is something that a program has to deliberately include in their contract in order
to ask the supplier to do the Cyber Test and Evaluation of even trusted suppliers
so that they can understand if there is risk or if there's a compromise occurring.
Another tool is to plan ahead to make sure you have the specialized tools,
techniques, and test personnel.
Hardware or software -- hardware analysis
and hardware assurance testing is a little bit different than software --
a lot different, frankly, than software assurance testing.
So, understanding what is needed and is an important tool to have in your toolbox.
Continuous iterative and targeted Cyber Test and Evaluation,
which we're going to talk about here.
Both contractors, I mean, the contractors and the developers need to be doing that.
And we also want to hold our -- ask our contractors to improve the design --
the engineering for resilience by being able to engineer a system that well
as my Apotek [phonetic] friend Blast [phonetic] likes to say is design the system
to be a honey badger system so that it doesn't care
if there is a compromise in the supply chain.
It has been designed to be able to withstand any compromise.
That's the holy grail of where we want to be.
It's a -- that's a big, big problem, though.
So, how does that system monitor, respond to, and recover in its capabilities
so that the mission and system won't be --
the compromises won't impact that mission is what I want to say.
All right.
Moving on to slide nine.
So, we propose Cyber Test and Evaluation to help reduce cyber supply chain risks.
And that requires some key things to do that.
First is the program needs to resource their government test teams
to have early engagement -- early assists from those government test teams.
They support the request for proposal and making sure
that contract language has cyber tests and evaluation in it.
Not just for supply chain, but in general.
And they have to ensure that the government will have data rights, access to observe if needed,
be able to collect the right data, monitor that test equipment,
and participate with the contractor in the testing
as an integrated test team if that's desired.
The test teams also support program protection planning activities
and the mission based cyber risk assessments.
And the test teams would be responsible for leveraging and helping to identify the tools
that can help discover mitigate and manage supply chain risk.
Then we move on to our intel community.
Another key partner to have early and continuously integrated with the program.
The intel community needs to have the detailed system and program information available
to them, so that they can provide that supply chain threat support,
because it's very difficult to do that analysis and to -- it's challenging because of the --
we've got someone with their hand raised.
It's very challenging for the intel community because it's again,
it's a difficult thing to see in advance.
You can't see it before it happens.
So, we have two organizations.
The Supply Chain Risk Management Threat Analysis Center under DIA, Defense Intelligence Agency,
and we have the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency that can assist programs
with their supply chain risk analysis and the Intel pieces of that.
So, the one thing I want to point out is
that our intelligence collection agencies have restrictions on collecting against US companies.
So, that limits a little bit of their ability to get the full insight that might be required.
And having your intel community support your mission based cyber risk assessments is a
tremendous help.
It helps the intel community learn and understand the system well enough to go back
and support the program better with better intel collection and analysis.
And then finally, we obviously want to talk about the Cyber T&E activities.
So, iterating for supply chain risk with Cyber T&E activities.
So, I'm moving on to Slide 10.
So, if you have an older version of the slide deck, if this might look a little different.
But this is our proposed new DOD Adaptive Cyber Test and Evaluation approach.
It replaces the six phases, the Cyber Test and Evaluation, and it should be published well,
within -- hopefully in FY22, we will see the guides come out.
There are two documents, the DOD Test and Evaluation guidebook,
we'll have a Cyber T&E focus area chapter, which we'll talk about these activities.
And that what to do is going to be supported by an update
to the DOD Cyber T&E Guide -- Companion Guide.
It's going to be called version three, which will discuss how to do these.
But we're going to focus on supply chain with these T&E activities.
So, as a stage setter, the big arrows going across show a continuum of tests from left
to right throughout the program's lifecycle.
And the big arrows are strategic activities.
The program sponsors the examine activity at the strategic level,
the plan activity at the strategic level, and the strategic conduct activities,
which are the mission based cyber risk assessment and the attack surface analysis.
And then any stakeholder can perform the strategic evaluate and report.
How's the program doing?
Are they on their Cyber T&E?
Are they working things right?
Right. So, that's the big strategic.
And then you notice in conduct there are these cycles inside.
These test cycles are meant to indicate multiple test events
that occur with each iteration of conduct.
So, when the when the prototyping is going on,
there should be some cyber testing evaluation going on when they're moving into EMD.
If we want to look at traditional major capability,
they will be a lot of testing going on and so on.
So, the testing is either contractor led or government led.
It can be focused on developmental objectives, operational objectives,
or integrated test objectives, which is optimal.
And they can be cooperative in nature or adversarial in nature.
So, that's the idea behind this.
It's meant to be adaptive to support any program cadence.
So, any adaptive acquisition pathway and I really hope
that this is helpful to the community writ large.
So, we look forward to your feedback on this activity.
So, let's break this down for supply chain.
So, I will be answering questions at the end I think is the is the plan.
All right.
So, examine at the strategic level.
For supply chain, the types of inputs needed to perform, examine, and these are not everything,
is the obviously the current program artifacts.
Everything about that you can have about missions, depending on where you are
in the lifecycle, you may not have enough information, but hopefully you have a concept
of operations, information on threats, information on the system design
and the architecture, any understanding
of what's critical program information components and functions.
Doing a mission decomposition, as Elly mentioned,
as part of your mission based cyber risk assessment will help with this.
But right now, it's just a matter of looking at everything.
Gathering all the information.
And the software bill of materials is an important piece because that's
where you get the ingredients in your software,
all the way down to every single open-source software component.
Over 80% of software these days is not originally coded.
It is reused software with a lot of open-source components.
So, that software bill of materials helps you understand what's in my software
and where are the vulnerabilities in those pieces and parts.
You also need, obviously a parts list to focus on the hardware side.
And what are you producing during this strategic examine activity?
You're producing what and why in the supply chain you want --
you the program need to focus on.
Where do you not have enough visibility into your supply chain?
Maybe you don't have a good illumination tool.
Where is there -- you've done supply chain risk management,
you've implemented a plan, but where is that risk?
Perhaps a manage because maybe you had a sole source supplier somewhere
down in the lower tiers where that part had to come from that particular supplier.
And then for the manage risk where you think you've got that under control,
then you might want to ask the supplier -- the prime contractor to do some testing just
as a spot check so that we don't blindly trust things
that we don't -- we shouldn't finely the trust.
Because of the dynamic nature of the supply chain, we should have some spot checks.
You also produce the supply chain elimination during examine.
It's easier if you have an automated tool.
There are automated tools to do that.
And it's -- then you also produce the attack surface characterization of your supply chain.
So, that's a big -- much bigger than the attack surface characterization of your system itself,
which isn't done until the conduct stage.
All right.
Moving on to slide 12.
The focus for examine -- I'm not going to read all these to you.
But you know, understanding the policies, understanding the risk management plans
that you're putting in place, both the supplier provided and the programs,
being able to have good visibility, being able to respond to the dynamic nature
of the supply chain, having good threat information from the intel community,
and sometimes open-source threat information is just as good.
And the intel community has to validate that of course, but that's good intel.
Understanding SolarWinds got hacked, you know, then how these -- how does that affect me?
And then the evidence of the manufacturer complying
with various standards that are provided.
So, that's an important thing to pay attention to.
And in particular, the DOD is working to publish cyber manufacturing readiness levels
for that manufacturing environment being able to ensure that that
that they've considered cyber in that environment.
That's really going to be a good thing and helpful.
So, being able to get the evidence of that.
Right now, those haven't been published, but they're coming.
And moving on to slide 13.
I'm still on examine, just so you know.
Let's focus on illuminating the supply chain step, that piece.
So, illuminating that ecosystem.
So, there on the right is that wheel of access.
And I, you know, you just pick one piece out of that wheel of access, and it has its own wheel
of access, and then one piece of that has its own wheel of access
and you can see how quickly the exponential growth of that supply chain shows up visually.
You can see that on the right.
Right. So, you have this high visibility at the system level, but you have no visibility
down there deeper in the supply chain.
And that's exactly where an adversary will hide.
Be able to get in and hide.
So, we want to illuminate all suppliers for software, firmware, hardware and data.
We need to understand the development, test, production, and manufacturing environments,
processes, and tools, the people, the technology, and the tools
and the way they do things, the processes.
Those are very important things to understand where your risk might need to be managed best.
Because if you don't understand those, then that's where the adversary --
that's the weakest point where the adversary can get in.
So, being able to use those illumination tools that can use AI to crawl the web
and map all these things, consider all the aspects, all those market forces
on the suppliers, everything that's going on that we as humans can't possibly comprehend
and synthesize ourselves, these tools, these illumination tools can do that for us.
And they can highlight where that risk is and how it changes over time.
So, that's a key piece to have.
I think our contractors need to have these kinds of tools in their tool bank,
and then the DOD should be also independently understanding the supply chain with these tools.
Moving on to slide 14.
So, looking at the attack surface characterization,
you need the supply chain illumination to do it and you need the detailed documentation.
And that means the designs, the contractor policies, their part acceptance testing,
how they're going to be doing that right?
Information on their environments, what security controls and plans, they are using.
Their third-party penetration testing, if they're doing any
of that against those environments.
And if you require these on contract, then you position yourself
to have a better handle on where to do the T&E.
So, the supply chain illumination informs the attack surface characterization,
as I said before, and as part of this examine step when you're producing
that attack surface characterization, you're going to slip -- when you go into conduct,
you're going to use this information
to inform individual test events, or the contractor is going to.
That's what you should expect.
So, that where do I need to do some Cyber T&E in this particular T&E event.
So which suppliers are providing which critical components and which --
what are the relationships between various elements of my supply chain?
What CMMC levels?
Are they -- did I need them to be a four but they're only a two,
because they're a sole supplier of that part.
That introduces risk.
So, that might be an area to focus on testing.
Are -- is there any foreign, you know, investment going on?
What if, I haven't said it enough, design, development,
tests and production facilities, processes ,and tools.
Make sure those are understood and ensuring that all facilities take into account the processes
and the tools and the people and how they play into that.
What kinds of facility controls are in place?
Physical and cyber controls, because the adversary can do physical penetration testing
as well.
And so that software bill of materials, understanding every single piece
of software in your overall system.
Every piece and part and piece.
It's very complex.
So, use the supply chain illumination, the criticality analyses, and those things to help
and focus on where is my attack surface that I need to pay attention
to for cyber tests and evaluation.
And I'm moving on to slide 16.
So, moving into strategic plan.
So, as you iterate through examine, plan, you can do examine more
than once before you can go to plan if needed.
And that sometimes is a good idea when it comes to Cyber T&E,
because things can change, and the threat can change.
So, for plan, what you take in is everything from examine.
Whatever the scope is that you produce, the what and the why to focus on for supply chain risk,
that illumination and the attack surface characterization.
In plan, if it's pre-RFP, you are producing contractual language
that supports supply chain Cyber T&E.
What and why do you need the contractor to test?
Who -- how do they flow that down or which things do you need
to be flowed down to their lower tiers?
How are they measuring a monitoring this software bill of materials?
Is it continuous?
Are they -- what are they required in terms of delivering for data and reporting?
And how often do they have to do those things?
What mitigation and response do they have in place to react to things
that might happen in the supply chain.
A SolarWinds compromise.
How do they respond to that?
A ransomware attack.
How do they respond to that?
And then whatever the risk management framework supply chain tests and evaluation controls
that you select in risk management framework,
making sure that those are included in the contract as well.
There are some good Cyber T&E controls for supply chain in the risk management framework.
If you're past RFP, then maybe you're looking
to update the contract language based on changes in threat.
And that's something to consider.
It might not be cost effective to do that.
So, it's best to get yourself off on the right foot to begin with.
And then the other aspect of plan when you iterate is updating or documenting
or updating the Cyber T&E supply chain risk, the Cyber T&E strategy for supply chain risk.
And that goes in the overall T&E strategy.
And it should be risk reduction driven based on the risk tolerance of the program.
What and why needs to be tested.
So, it goes in whatever the T&E strategy
for the appropriate pathway that the program is following.
It should specify who, what sort of tiers, when, and how often that testing needs to happen,
or is planned to happen, where is it going to be happening, and sort of a brief description
of how the testing is expected to happen.
Obviously, you're not going to get into test plan level.
This is a T&E strategy, it should be very strategic,
but making sure that you've documented what you're going to do so that you can pay attention
to those key things in the supply chain.
I'm going on to slide 17, the conduct phase.
So, conduct -- well, it's not phase.
Conduct activity.
So, the -- in the conduct activity, the program, and hopefully the contractor,
perform the mission based cyber risk assessments,
and it should have a supply chain focus.
And then they conduct those activities for each of the test events.
So, the test teams are responsible for this iteration that you see
in the circle inside the diagram on the bottom of this chart.
So, they will examine the supply chain attack surface and the intelligence relevant
to the test event they're getting ready to do.
What and why do I need to focus on with respect to supply chain in this event.
Write -- include in your test plan,
how you're going to assess the supply chain components that you're testing.
Then they conduct that event.
And I have some examples, yes, on the next slide.
And do that assurance testing for the supply chain assurance.
And then they go and evaluate the data and they're going to write their results
with recommendations that all gets into this cumulative body of evidence.
So, the program is responsible for having a place to store all this kind of data,
